cards.summary: Edit-interface choice measurably moves success, but the strongest numbers come from weak or older models and from the format's authors; for capable 2025-26 models the gap between sensible formats (str_replace vs hashline vs udiff) is single digits and model-specific. The Aider 20%->61% figure is a laziness benchmark on GPT-4 Turbo, not general coding.

contrarian.claim: Structured/format-constrained output degrades reasoning (original), later rebutted: the drop came from unequal prompts and a weak answer parser, not the format
contrarian.who: Tam et al. (Appier) vs Will Kurt (dottxt)
contrarian.note: Rebuttal re-ran 3 tasks; gaps tiny (GSM8K 0.77 vs 0.78); authored by a vendor of structured generation. The original paper itself I only saw via search summaries, not opened. Concerns free-text answers vs JSON, not code edit formats; irrelevant to tool-call JSON on 2026 models.

contrarian.claim: No single edit format dominates; best choice depends on task (generation vs application) and model size
contrarian.modelEra: GPT-4.1, Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-Coder; non-reasoning, greedy
contrarian.note: Search-replace best for diff generation on large models (Claude 4 Sonnet EM 0.94); udiff best for apply; proxy tasks, not agent end-to-end.

contrarian.claim: Hashline edit interface beats patch by ~15-20pp on average across 16 models but beats plain str_replace by only ~0-11pp, near zero or negative for GPT-5.2 Codex (-0.4), Grok 4 Fast (-0.4), DeepSeek V3.2 (-8.3); Claude Sonnet 4.5 +3.3 vs str_replace
contrarian.modelEra: 2026-era (Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2 Codex, Gemini 3 Flash, Kimi K2.5)
contrarian.note: Fetched via a redirect from blog.can.ac. Self-run, author promotes the format, mutation-reversal tasks, partial reporting, internal inconsistencies. Cuts both ways: format matters vs patch, but str_replace (the Claude convention) is already close for capable models. Supports 'format matters, shrinking with capability'.

failures.what: Aider's 20%->61% is on a bespoke 89-task refactoring 'laziness' suite (checks code was not replaced by comments), GPT-4 Turbo gpt-4-1106; GPT-4-0613 26%->59%. Author calls it not a rigorous correctness test.
failures.modelEra: GPT-4 Turbo (2023); likely does not transfer to 2026 models
failures.whatItShows: Format effect is real for a lazy model but scoped to one failure mode; the claim 'format > stronger prompting' was also only tested against emotional/tip prompts.

conditions: Holds strongly for weak/small/older models and for mismatched formats (e.g. apply_patch given to non-GPT models: patch failure 46-51% for GLM-4.7, Grok 4).
Weak for frontier models when using their native convention (str_replace for Claude, apply_patch for GPT): differences within a few points.
Check format against the specific model family, not a universal winner.
cards.conclusion: For Claude 5-class models, use the vendor-native str_replace-style tool and do not expect large gains from exotic formats; the 'format over prompt' slogan rests on GPT-4-era Aider data and author-run 2026 benchmarks. It remains a good rule to fix format mismatches (e.g. do not use unified diff or apply_patch for a model not trained on it) and to constrain only the final answer, not the reasoning. I found no 2026 controlled study of edit-format sensitivity specifically for Claude 5. A held-out edit-format ablation on the harness's own tasks with Sonnet/Opus 5 would settle it.

cards.summary: SWE-agent's own ablation supports lint-gated rejection (18.0% -> 15.0% without lint, GPT-4 Turbo), but it is a 3pp single-run effect on SWE-bench Lite with a 2024 model. Practitioner sources and LangChain's 2026 work show guardrails/loop detectors help weaker or current models yet are described as workarounds that may become unnecessary; I found no rigorous study showing lint-gating harms, only plausible failure modes.

contrarian.claim: Guardrails like loop detection and pre-completion checklists are workarounds for current model weaknesses, may not help if the model believes its approach is right, and are expected to become unnecessary as models improve
contrarian.note: Same post shows harness changes (including loop detection) lifted Terminal Bench 2.0 52.8->66.5, so it supports gating while hedging its longevity. No held-out evaluation; overfitting warning included.

contrarian.claim: Harness complexity growth over 35 releases brought no statistically significant gain on SWE-bench Verified subset and ~2x tokens/tool calls
contrarian.modelEra: fixed LLM in Qwen Code CLI, 50 tasks
contrarian.note: Not specific to rejection/retry; shows added harness machinery often does not pay off. Small sample (50 tasks); Verified has validity issues.

failures.what: SWE-agent paper reports 51.7% of trajectories had a failed edit; after one failed edit the chance of eventually succeeding fell from 90.5% to 57.2%; cascading failed edits explain 23.4% of unresolved failures; the guardrail constrains edit order (must edit references in same action).
failures.whatItShows: Shows the cost the gate addresses and one stated drawback (edit-order constraint). The 3pp lint ablation is single-model, no confidence interval; GPT-4-era failure rates do not predict Claude 5 edit error rates.

conditions: Value tracks the model's base edit-error rate, which is far lower in 2026 models.
Gate must be per-final-state or return actionable errors; per-edit syntax gating can block valid multi-step refactors (plausible, only anecdotal sources found).
Retry caps should be tied to no-progress detection (same failing check, same diff), not raw count.
cards.conclusion: Specific, actionable rejection feedback is well supported as a design principle and cheap, but its measured benefit comes from GPT-4 Turbo and shrinks as models stop making syntax-breaking edits. I found no credible study showing lint-gating or retry caps hurting 2026 models; the loop/blocked-state concerns are anecdotal. In a script-driven harness, keep rejection with reasons, prefer gating on final state and no-progress caps over fixed low retry counts. A Claude 5 ablation of the gate (on/off, same tasks, multiple runs) would change the verdict.

cards.summary: mini-swe-agent's bash-only result is a credible controlled-comparison baseline, and a small 2026 pilot found it matches native harnesses, but its headline 74-75% sits on SWE-bench Verified, which OpenAI declared no longer meaningful (59.4% of audited failing tasks had tests rejecting correct solutions; contamination). Harness effects of 5-20pp on Terminal-Bench 2.x show scaffolds do matter on other benchmarks, while the best controlled studies find harness differences on pass rate are small and tokens/cost differ far more.

contrarian.claim: SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding ability: flawed tests (>=59.4% of audited hard problems) and training-data contamination; OpenAI stopped reporting it and recommends SWE-bench Pro
contrarian.who: OpenAI (reported via Gigazine; I did not open OpenAI's own page)
contrarian.note: Secondary report of an OpenAI audit; progress slowed to ~6% over six months. Undermines the 75% number as evidence about scaffold value.

contrarian.claim: Same model, different harness: GPT-5.5 83.4% in Codex CLI vs 78.2% in Terminus 2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1; Opus 4.7 68.9 vs 66.1 (Claude Code vs Terminus 2)
contrarian.note: Fetched page itself has inconsistent gap figures (7 vs 5.2 points); secondary blog; leaderboard entries not controlled for effort or budget.

contrarian.claim: Harness engineering alone lifted a fixed model on Terminal Bench 2.0 from 52.8% to 66.5%
contrarian.note: Vendor, single benchmark of 89 tasks, no held-out check. Added verify-before-exit and context-injection middleware, i.e. richer scaffold beats plain loop on long tasks.

contrarian.claim: Position paper: benchmarks fuse model+harness+environment; Opus 4.6 on Terminal-Bench ranges 58.0% (Claude Code) to 79.8% (ForgeCode); 4-10pp swings on SWE-bench
contrarian.note: Position paper with no new experiments, relies on leaderboards/blogs, authors promote their own harness.

failures.what: Controlled 300-trial study (Terminal-Bench Pro, 50 tasks, Goose/OpenCode/OpenHands-SDK, Qwen 3.6 Plus & MiniMax M2.5): pass-rate differences 0-8pp mostly not significant, but tokens per solved task differed ~40x (28K vs ~1.15M).
failures.whatItShows: Scaffold complexity mostly changes cost and failure mode, not accuracy, at this sample size; supports 'simple is not worse' but low power (1 task = 2pp).

failures.what: DeepSWE fixed-harness pilot: n=10 SWE-bench Pro tasks, mini-swe-agent equal or better than native (Opus 4.7 50% vs 40%, GPT-5.5 40/40, Gemini 3.1 Pro 40 vs 20) at comparable tokens; authors say within noise and mini-swe-agent's prompt maps onto the grader, so no ranking of production harnesses.
failures.whatItShows: Only rules out a large handicap from bash-only; routing edits via bash may hold some families below native ceiling (their own limitation).

failures.what: Scale SWE-Bench Pro V2: for the strongest open-weight models harness (mini-swe-agent, Pi, OpenCode) did not change outcomes, cost varied more; public Pro had reward hacking/leakage, 89 tasks removed; public-private gap 17.8% for Opus 5.
failures.whatItShows: Pro is also not clean; harness-insensitivity there is measured on open-weight models, and charts were not readable in my fetch.

failures.what: Longitudinal study: 35 Qwen Code releases on fixed LLM, no significant SWE-bench gain, ~2x tokens.
failures.whatItShows: More scaffold != better on Verified subset (50 tasks).

conditions: Bash-only is a good baseline for model comparison and when tasks are short, well-specified, single-repo.
Richer harnesses win on long-horizon/terminal tasks where verification, context injection and time management matter (Terminal-Bench 2.x gains of 5-20pp reported, mostly vendor/blog sourced).
The 75% figure should not be used as evidence either way because Verified is contaminated/flawed.
cards.conclusion: Net: 'a minimal bash loop is hard to beat on accuracy' is partly supported by controlled 2026 studies (small pass-rate differences, big cost differences), but the cited 75% number is on a benchmark OpenAI has retired, and Terminal-Bench evidence shows verification/context middleware can add several points to double digits. For a script-driven SDLC harness the lesson is to keep the model-facing loop simple while owning verification and navigation in scripts, and to measure cost per solved task. Evidence on Claude 5 specifically is thin (Scale V2 mentions Opus 5 only for the public/private gap). A controlled Claude 5 comparison of bash-only vs the harness on long-horizon tasks, with multiple seeds, would change the verdict.
